extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century literary humor; readers of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century humorous/prose essay mixing personal anecdote, mock-legal renunciation, and reflective comic meditation on aging and habits, aimed at general readers. The piece models techniques of light satire, self-deprecation, and conversational lecturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary honesty regarding originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal renunciation of claim to being the first author of a simile/comparison when evidence of prior use appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author presents a mock-legal instrument: he 'do hereby renounce all claim to being considered the first person who gave utterance to a certain simile... relating to the pupil of the eye on the one part and the mind of the bigot on the other.' He relinquishes 'all glory and profit,' allows editors and critics 'to retract or qualify any opinion predicated on the supposition that I was the sole and undisputed author,' and requests that those who have implied impropriety 'have the manliness forthwith to retract.' This models explicit public acknowledgement or relinquishment when originality is doubtful, and suggests authors should disclaim originality or note coincidences when suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: If an idea may be borrowed, disclaim or acknowledge coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writer suspects an idea may not be original, they should disclose the coincidence rather than claim sole authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states: 'If I had even suspected that the idea in question was borrowed, I should have disclaimed originality, or mentioned the coincidence, as I once did in a case where I had happened to hit on an idea of Swift’s.' Also: 'It is impossible to tell, in a great many cases, whether a comparison which suddenly suggests itself is a new conception or a recollection.' Practical guidance: explicitly disclaim originality or mention known antecedents when there is reasonable doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to younger readers about suitable timing for material
rubrics_metrics.description: Some material (reflections, lectures, essays) may not be appropriate or comprehensible to younger readers and can be deferred until later life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prefatory aside: 'I would suggest to young persons that they should pass over it for the present, and read, instead of it, that story about the young man who was in love...' and 'Perhaps, if such young people will lay the number aside, and take it up ten years, or a little more, from the present time, they may find something in it for their advantage.' Guidance implied: tailor reading (and perhaps writing) to audience maturity; indicate when material is intended for older readers.
